en: Homage to the glorious Hevajra.
In the language of India: *Abhisamayakrama-nāma*. In the language of Tibet: *Mngon par rtogs pa'i rim pa zhes bya ba* (The Stages of Clear Realization). Homage to the glorious Hevajra!
The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the precious *Hevajra-tantra*, which emerged from Śrī Oḍḍiyāna, is now explained.
The *Abhisamaya* of the Jewel of the *Śrī-Ādyanasamudgata-janma-vajra-tantra* shall now be explained:

There are thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*) that carry the bodhicitta, whose nature consists of both the conventional and the ultimate. Among them, three are primary: *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*. *Lalanā* has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). [*Rasanā* has the nature of method (*upāya*). *Avadhūtī* is the form of the non-dual reality within the *yoni-cakra*.

The thirty-two channels through which the bodhicitta flows possess the nature of both the conventional and the ultimate. Among these, there are three principal ones: lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī. Lalanā has the nature of wisdom (prajñā); rasanā has the nature of method (upāya); and avadhūtī is the form of non-dual reality within the wheel of the birth-place.

Lalanā carries *akṣobhya*; rasanā carries blood; avadhūtī carries the *bodhicitta*. Lalanā is that which carries the unmoving; rasanā is that which carries the blood; avadhūtī is that which carries the *bodhicitta*. Lalanā is the extreme subtlety of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); rasanā is the non-proliferation (*aprapañca*) of all phenomena; avadhūtī is of an indivisible nature.

(1) The extreme subtlety of all phenomena is the *brkyang ma* [lalanā]; the non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) of all phenomena is the *ro ma* [rasanā]; and that which has the nature of being indivisible is the *kun ’dar ma* [avadhūtī].
The locations and natures of these thirty-two channels are now described.
The locations and natures of those two channels, the *rTza sum cu* and the *rTza gnyis po*, shall now be described:
on the big toe of the left foot is *Abhedyā*, because she is devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatvāt*).
On the big toe of the left foot is *Abhedyā*, because she is devoid of intrinsic nature.
In the shank is Sūkṣmarūpā, because her nature is that of the space element.
The divine one on the left thigh is so called because she consists of the five desires;
[is it not] because she consists of the five objects of desire? Because she possesses the nature of the five desires.

On the left side of the womb, the channel is Vāmā; because she possesses the power of the left reality, she is the Wisdom (*prajñā*) that holds the excellent suchness. At the navel is Vāminī, whose nature is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of Mahāmudrā.
The many short *lte ba ru* syllables have the nature of being the concordant result (*nisyanda*) of the Great King.

On the left side of the pericarp of the heart is Kūrmajā, because she has the form of the union of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and nirvana (*nirvāṇa*). On the left side of the pericarp of the heart is Kūrmajā, because she has the form of the union of cyclic existence and nirvana.
On the left breast is the meditation on Bhāvakī as great bliss;
on the left side of the throat is the consecration through the descent of stainlessness.

On the left side of the neck is Doṣā, because she purifies [the body] by means of blows with the palms and so forth. On the palm of the left hand is Doṣā, because she effects transformation by means of slaps with the palms and so forth.
In the lower [vagina],
she carries the excrement because great bliss enters;
in the cheeks, she is the Mother because she reveals the *ālaya*.
The three *mkhur tsos* [cheeks] are for the sake of seeing all four;
in the left eye is Sarvārī, whose nature is the bathing of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
In the left eye is Sarvārī, whose nature is the bathing of great bliss.
At the root of the left throat is Śītadā, because she originates from wind;
on the left side of the head is Uṣṇā, because she is radiant with fire.
On the left side of the cloth is Cāṇḍālī, because she possesses fire;
on the left side of the Great Vajradhara at the crown of the head is Lalanā, because her nature is to sport.
At the crown of the head, on the left side of the Great Vajradhara, is Rasā, because her nature is to be playful.
In front is Avadhūtī, because she is free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca). On the right is Rasanā, because she delights in flavors.
To the right is the desire for enjoyment;
from behind is the authority, because it is the authority of the body and so forth.
On the right side of the head, she is black in color because Akṣobhya is black;
on the root of the right ear, she is the Universal One who follows everywhere.
RNA BA G-YAS (Right Ear): Because it follows all [the others] as the general head.

PA'I RTZA BAR (In the center of the forehead): Because she is the bestower of the cause (*hetudāyikā*), being the causal condition (*kāraṇa*). MIG G-YAS PA LA (In the right eye): She is Hetudāyikā because she has become the efficient cause (*kārana*).
On the cheek is the "separation" [mudrā], because it is devoid of the joy of union;
on the upper lip is the "beloved," because of the continuous attachment to the abode everywhere.
Ya is Siddhā on the lips because she strikes all the places [of articulation];
Gaṇe is Siddhā on the throat because her nature is beginningless.
The right hand is that of the Fire-god (Pāvakī), because it expands the aesthetic flavor of the erotic (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
On the right breast is Sumanā, for the sake of attaining the "good mind" (*sumanā*) that arises as the fruit of the body;
on the right side of the heart is Trivṛtā, because she consists of the nature of body, speech, and mind.
On the right side of the heart is Sumskor-ma, because she is the embodiment of Body,
Speech, and Mind. On the region of the right hip is ’Dod-ma, because she is fond of desire.
The "House" (geha) is the womb (yoni), because it is the abode of all beings; and the "Wide One" (urū) is Caṇḍālī, because she pervades everything through great bliss.
Kātyāyanī is at the shanks because she cuts through all obstacles;
at the shanks is Kātyāyanī because she eliminates all obstructing spirits (*vighna*).

On the right thumb is Māradāyikā, because all suffering does not enter [there]. In the thirty-two channels, according to their respective locations and in both direct and reverse order, are the sixteen syllables and the days beginning with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).

In the two channels of the head, neck, and heart, there are sixteen syllables according to their respective locations; and on the first day and so forth, they follow the sequence of the days in both forward and reverse order.
These channels are the transformation of the three realms, having been transformed by great bliss through their nature as body and the other [aggregates].

The *rtza de* (channels) are the complete transformation of the three realms of existence; they are the complete transformation into great bliss by way of the nature of the *sku la* (body, speech, and mind), and so forth.
*Āli* refers to the series beginning with the letter *a*; *kāli* refers to the series beginning with the letter *ka*. *Āli* is the form of *ā* and so forth; *kāli* is the form of *ka* and so forth.
The vajra, lotus, method, wisdom, dharma, enjoyment, emanation, and the innate; the supreme, the free from passion, and the mind, speech, and body.
The vajra and the lotus; method and wisdom; the dharma, the enjoyment, the emanation, the innate, the supreme, and the free from passion; and the mind, speech, and body.

Thus by me: the syllable *E* is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), joy (*ānanda*), and the goddess Locanā; the syllable *Vaṃ* is the vajra, the signless (*animitta*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and Māmakī; the syllable *Ma* is heat (*ūṣma*), the wishless (*apraṇihitā*), the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), and Pāṇḍarā; the syllable *Yā* is fluidity (*dravatva*), the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the innate (*sahaja*), and Tārā.

The aspect of *Ā* is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), emptiness, joy, and the goddess Locanā. The aspect of *Vām* is the vajra, the signless, supreme joy, and Māmakī. The aspect of *Mā* is greatness, wishlessness, the joy of separation from passion, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī. The aspect of *Yā* is the nature of moisture and... [310b] manifestly...
"Adopted, co-emergent, and Tārā.

In the *nirmāṇacakra* of the *yonau*, there are sixty-four petals; the thirty-two syllables beginning with *ka* [and those ending with *kṣa*] arranged in direct and reverse order constitute the sixty-four syllables.

Regarding the sixty-four petals of the wheel that emanates into the place of birth, there are sixty-four syllables—thirty-two such as *ka* and so forth, arranged in forward and reverse order. On each of the four lotus petals and so on, the sixty-four petals are the natural transformation of the letters of the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), such as Locanā and the others, which are their purified forms.

The wheel of the abode is produced from *par*. At the heart is the eight-petaled dharma wheel (*dharmacakra*), upon which appear the eight syllables *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*, consisting of the primary elements and those derived from them; these are extremely subtle forms. It is an eight-petaled lotus. At the throat is the enjoyment wheel (*saṃbhogacakra*) with sixteen petals, upon which appear: *a ā aḥ ai aiḥ au auḥ ri rī li lī e ai o au am aḥ*; it is empty.

The purification of the sixteen [pīṭhas] is the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the sixteen-year-old [consort], who is the nature of the Saṃbhogakāya. She herself is the sixteen-petaled wheel of the Saṃbhogakāya. At the crown of the head, upon the thirty-two petals of the Mahāsukha-cakra, are: *ka kha ga gha ṅa*, *ca cha ja jña ña*, *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*, *ta tha da dha na*, *pa pha ba bha ma*, *ya ra la va*, *śa ṣa sa*.

The thirty-two purified marks of a Great Being consist of the following: the four moments renowned as the four wheels are the moment of variety, the moment of maturation, the moment of enjoyment, and the moment free from characteristics. The four truths are suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. The four realities are the reality of self, the reality of phenomena, the reality of suchness, and the reality of the ultimate.

The reality of mantra, the reality of the deity, and the reality of primordial wisdom. The four joys are the joy of delight, the joy of supreme rapture, the joy of the absence of passion, and the innate joy. The four schools are the Sthaviras, the Sarvāstivādins, the Saṃmitīyas, and the Mahāsāṃghikas. These [are characterized by] the momentary, the truth, and...

These very [elements] are established in four states by way of their differentiation, their nature as small, medium, and the remainder, and by being exceedingly great: the left moon, the right sun, the subtle *āli*, the subtle *kāli*, and the gross *kāli*. The sixteen breaths are the sheep, the ox, the ram, *karkaṭa*, the lion, the maiden, Libra, and...

The sin (sdig pa), the bow (gzhu), the makara (chu srin), the water jar (bum pa), the fish (nya), the waning moon (zla ba gzas zin), the waning sun (nyi ma gzas zin), the cessation of the bindu (thig le 'gog pa), and the cessation of space (nam mkha' 'gog pa)—these are the sixteen digits (spom po) of the transference. Alternatively, through the distinction between the leftward and rightward revolutions of the semen, there occurs a transference into the sixteen locations. On the first day, at the big toe, there is the form of *ā*.

Dang, for the two [fingers] of the hands, the form of *āḥ*; for the three [fingers] of the separation, the form of *ai*; for the four [fingers] at the place of birth, the form of *āi*; for the five [fingers] at the navel, the form of *au*; for the six [fingers] at the heart, the form of *āu*; for the seven [fingers] at the breasts, the form of *ri*; for the eight [fingers] at the throat, the form of *rī*; for the nine [fingers] at the tips of the hands, the form of *li*; for the ten [fingers] at the eyebrows, the form of *lī*; for the eleven [fingers] at the eyes, the form of *e*; for the ears...

In the twelve spokes of the heart wheel, there is the form of Aiḥ; in the thirteen, at the forehead, the form of Aoḥ; in the fourteen at the crown of the head, the form of Aūḥ; and in the full left and right flanks, Ām and Āḥ.

The transition occurs through the extremely subtle aspect of that very same breath. Regarding the sixty-four finger-joints (*aṅgula*), one should take the finger-joints by way of the aspects of time: the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the fifteen days of the day, the nine planets (*graha*), and the twelve divisions. For both night and day, there are sixty finger-joints, and within those very [periods], there is exhaustion.

"There are four *phel ba*s; for that very reason, sixty-four *dbyi gu*s should be retained according to time. Alternatively, through the distinction between ultimate and conventional truth regarding wisdom and method, one should retain the *dbyi gu*s by means of the sixteen transformations (*pariṇāma*) of the pure states residing in each of those, [further divided] by the transformations of the intoxicants (*madana*). These are the thirty-two *rtsa*s. All of these are the wheel."
The Summaries of the Four [Chapters]. Furthermore, the four are as follows: the blazing of Caṇḍālī at the navel is absorbed into Mahāmudrā.
This concludes the *Abhisamayakrama* (Stages of Clear Realization).
